title: The Second Declension — Masculine
subtitle: dominus, servus, puer, vir.
objectives: Decline second-declension masculine nouns ending in -us, -er, and -ir.
Recognize the vocative singular in -e and distinguish it from the nominative.
Translate sentences using second-declension nouns as subjects, objects, and possessors.
Understand the stem-change in nouns like puer and ager.

sections.heading: The second declension: masculine nouns
sections.body:
The second declension contains masculine and neuter nouns. Today, the masculine. Most end in -us in the nominative singular. A few end in -er or -ir. The paradigm:

          Singular    Plural
  Nom.    dominus     dominī
  Gen.    dominī      dominōrum
  Dat.    dominō      dominīs
  Acc.    dominum     dominōs
  Abl.    dominō      dominīs
  Voc.    domine      dominī

The vocative singular is the only form that differs from the nominative in its ending: -e instead of -us. Cicero addresses a man named Marcus as 'Marce', not 'Marcus'.

sections.heading: Nouns in -er: puer and ager
sections.body:
Some second-declension masculine nouns end in -er in the nominative. There are two patterns:

  puer (boy) — the e survives in all forms: puer, puerī, puerō, puerum, puerō, puerī, puerōrum, etc.
  ager (field) — the e drops after the nominative: ager, agrī, agrō, agrum, agrō, agrī, agrōrum, etc.

The genitive singular tells you which pattern a noun follows. If the genitive is puerī, the e survives. If it is agrī, the e drops. The dictionary always gives both nominative and genitive for this reason.

Caesar writes: agrī vastābantur. — The fields were being laid waste. 'agrī' is nominative plural, subject of the passive verb.

Cicero writes: līberī meī. — My children. 'līberī' (the plural of līber, a poetic word for 'child') is nominative plural.

sections.heading: Examples from Caesar and Vergil
sections.body:
dominus servum vocat. — The master calls the slave.
servus dominum timet. — The slave fears the master.
filius virī fortis est. — The son of the man is brave.
puerō librum dō. — I give a book to the boy.
cum puerīs lūdō. — I play with the boys.
Mārce, venī! — Marcus, come! (vocative)

Vergil writes: arma virumque canō. — I sing of arms and the man. 'virum' is accusative singular, direct object of 'canō'.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Decline servus (slave) in all cases, singular and plural.

items.prompt: What is the difference between puer and ager?
items.answer: puer keeps the e in all forms; ager drops it after the nominative.

items.prompt: How do you address Marcus directly?

words.gloss: The boy plays in the field.
The son of the man is brave.
